text: Here is an answer that would lose the mark. Our framing: a gene controlling cell division has mutated; explain how a tumour can form. Read this answer. Look at the word mitosis. It is tempting, since a tumour is built by cells dividing. Beyond the scheme, mitosis also repairs healthy tissue: naming it does not explain a tumour. What is missing is control. In this question the mutation is supplied; the marks are for its consequences. Loss of cell-cycle control allows repeated uncontrolled division, which builds a mass of abnormal cells. The scheme awards two marks for any two credited consequences. It does not require an extra named gene, a checkpoint protein or how the mutation arose. So, in place: the mutation causes loss of control of the cell cycle, so the cell divides repeatedly by mitosis without control, producing a mass of abnormal cells, a tumour.
